title: How to Keep a Sabbath
excerpt: Sabbath is not a reward for finishing your work. The work is never finished. Sabbath is the weekly declaration that the world will keep turning without you, because it was never being held up by you.
body:
We are exhausted in a way our grandparents would not recognize, and we wear it like a badge. Busyness has become the proof that we matter. To rest feels like falling behind, and to fall behind feels like disappearing. Into this God speaks one of the strangest and most generous commands ever given to a tired people. Stop. One day in seven, stop.

Sabbath is the command we are most proud of breaking. We treat it as the optional one, the relic, the rule that applied to a slower age. But it sits in the Ten Commandments between idolatry and murder, and it is the longest of the ten. God spent more words protecting your rest than protecting your life. That should make us pause.

## Remember why it exists

God gave two reasons for the Sabbath, and both are worth holding. In Exodus, he points back to creation. He made the world in six days and rested on the seventh, not because he was tired, but to establish a rhythm woven into reality itself. In Deuteronomy, he points back to slavery. You were slaves in Egypt, worked without rest, and I brought you out. Sabbath is the proof that you are not a slave anymore.

That second reason cuts deep. To refuse to rest is, in a sense, to return to Egypt, to let work become the master that owns every hour. Sabbath is a weekly act of resistance against that slavery. One day a week, you are not what you produce.

## Pick the day and protect it

For most Christians the day is Sunday, gathered around worship and the resurrection, though the principle matters more than the particular day. Whatever day you choose, choose it on purpose and put a wall around it. Sabbath does not happen by drifting into a free afternoon. It happens because you decided in advance that this block of time is set apart and you defended it against the thousand things that wanted it.

The defense is the hard part. Work will always present itself as urgent. There will always be one more email, one more errand, one more reason this week is the exception. Treat the exception with deep suspicion. The week that most insists you cannot rest is usually the week you most need to.

## Stop, and then delight

Sabbath has two movements. First, you stop. You cease the work, the striving, the productivity, the low hum of usefulness. Put the laptop in a drawer. Leave the lawn unmowed. Let the inbox sit. This will feel wrong at first, almost physically wrong, and that discomfort is itself a diagnosis of how deeply work has gotten its hooks in you.

Then, having stopped, you delight. Sabbath is not merely the absence of work. It is the presence of joy. Eat a long meal. Take a slow walk. Sleep without an alarm. Be with people you love and do not check the time. Read something that has no purpose but pleasure. Worship without rushing off. The day is meant to be a feast, not a fast, a foretaste of the rest that is coming when all the striving is finally over.

## Plan ahead so rest is possible

Here is a practical truth the tradition understood well. A good Sabbath requires preparation. The Israelites gathered twice the manna on the sixth day so they would not have to work on the seventh. You will need to do the same. Run the errands, do the cooking, finish the urgent task the day before, so that when the Sabbath comes you can actually rest rather than spending it putting out fires. Rest is the fruit of forethought.

## Do not turn it into a new law

Jesus was sharp with those who had turned the Sabbath into a cage of rules, counting steps and forbidding mercy. The Sabbath was made for man, he said, not man for the Sabbath. So do not weaponize this against yourself or your family. If your toddler needs feeding, feed her. If your neighbor needs help, help. The point is freedom, gladness, and trust, not a new ledger of violations to feel guilty about. Hold it with grace.

## This week

Choose one day in the next seven. The day before, do the preparing, the shopping, the cooking, the urgent thing, so the day itself is clear. On the Sabbath, put work away entirely, no email, no productivity, and do three things that bring you genuine delight and one thing that is simply worship. At the end of the day, notice how hard it was to stop. That difficulty is the measure of how much you needed it.

The world spun for billions of years before you arrived and will spin after you are gone. Sabbath is the day you remember, with relief, that holding it up was never your job.
